This report summarizes the key technological developments from the Athena project with new tools and resources for airports, as well as the lab testing and emulation results that validate system performance to de-risk technology solutions prior to field demonstrations and deployments. 1 This report is available at no cost from the National Laboratory of the Rockies at www.nlr.gov/publications. 1 Airport Electrification Planning As airport operations evolve and electrification expands, it is important to forecast electrical loads across airport sectors and understand their potential impact. This section outlines the potential load growth at airport rental car centers (RCCs), possible impacts from increasing electrical demand from charging electric vehicles (EVs), and potential solutions to mitigate impacts and reduce costs. 1.1 Growing Loads Among airport operation sectors, RCCs undergoing electrification with the adoption of EVs might result in outstanding electrical loads due to the volume of vehicles requiring charging upon return and the traditional rental car business model. For example, in 2024, Los Angeles International Airport saw approximately 189,000 rental transactions per month, or 6,000 per day [6]. Moreover, the rental car business model is dictated by minimum vehicle inventory, which results in a short turnaround time between a vehicle’s return and the next rental pickup, also defined as “dwell time” [7]. Anecdotal evidence suggests that 25% of vehicles have a dwell time at the RCC of 1 hour or less. Under these assumptions, and in advanced electrification scenarios, a significant fraction of the vehicles returned to the RCC would require charging using high-power DC electric vehicle supply equipment (EVSE) typically rated at 350 kW, which can charge an EV from 20% to 80% state of charge (SOC) in 30 minutes or less. Initial analysis assuming the use of 350-kW EVSE and 10% fleet electrification at Dallas Fort Worth International Airport—amounting to 367 rental drop-off events per day—estimated peak electrical loads as high as 5 MW, which could require electrical distribution upgrades amounting to $13.5 million [3]. 1.2 Aeroportal Forecasts The Athena team developed the Aeroportal to enable airport stakeholders and partners to access results generated by the National Laboratory of the Rockies’s (NLR’s) high-fidelity optimization and simulation models within an online, accessible interface [8]. The Aeroportal can be used to estimate power requirements and cost across different airport transportation sectors, including RCCs, ground support equipment, transportation network companies, and parking. Users can interactively select scenario parameters such as expected vehicle demand volume, return and target SOC, and utility tariffs, and in turn estimate total cost, peak load, and grid stability. In addition to the grid-only (business-as-usual) scenario, the Aeroportal also reports solutions that include optimally sized battery energy storage systems (BESS), which considerably decrease costs and grid upgrade requirements and improve grid stability. The BESS solutions can be compared with the grid-only solutions to understand the savings produced by this technology under specific scenario assumptions, which can amount to millions of dollars and tens of megawatts in peak load reduction.
